Compression & Filters

Source: vignettes/articles/compression.Rmd
compression.Rmd

One of the most powerful features of HDF5 is its ability to compress data transparently. When you read a compressed dataset, the HDF5 library automatically decompresses it for you. This can lead to significant savings in storage space and faster I/O performance.

hdf5lib provides built-in support for gzip and szip compression natively, and additionally bundles an extensive suite of high-performance modern filter plugins. They use the same filter IDs and parameter layouts as Python’s h5py with hdf5plugin, and the package’s interoperability tests (tests/interop) check both directions: files written through hdf5lib read in h5py, and the other way round. Two exceptions: the standalone Snappy filter (32003) is not part of hdf5plugin, and Blosc2 datasets with 1-D chunks written by hdf5lib 2.2.0.0 or earlier cannot be read by hdf5plugin (rewrite them with a newer hdf5lib).

Terminology

To navigate HDF5 compression effectively, it is helpful to understand the specific terminology used throughout this guide and the broader HDF5 ecosystem:

  • Filter: A function in the HDF5 data pipeline that transforms data before it is written to disk or after it is read from disk.

  • Pre-filter: A specific type of filter (like Bitshuffle) designed to rearrange bytes to make the data more mathematically compressible before handing it off to the main compressor.

  • Compressor / Codec: The algorithm (e.g., Zstd, LZ4, ZFP) that actually shrinks the physical data footprint.

  • Plugin: An external, dynamically loaded library (e.g., a .so or .dll file) that provides the HDF5 library with the code needed to execute a filter that isn’t built into the core library.

  • Mode: A specific operational setting for a compressor (e.g., ZFP’s “Fixed Accuracy” mode or LZ4’s “High Compression” mode).

Fundamental Requirements for HDF5 Compression

Before configuring any filter, you must understand the fundamental rules of HDF5 compression:

  1. Chunking is Mandatory: Compression in HDF5 requires the data to be stored in “chunks.” You must define a chunk size for your dataset using H5Pset_chunk(). Applying a filter to a contiguous dataset will fail.

  2. Filter Registration (Plugins Only): If you are using any of the bundled plugins (Zstd, LZ4, Blosc, etc.), they must be registered globally in your R session. You should do this exactly once from your package’s R_init_<pkgname>() entry point using hdf5lib_register_all_filters(), and tear them down in R_unload_<pkgname>() with hdf5lib_destroy_all_filters(). Registering filters per-I/O operation will severely degrade performance. See the Getting Started guide for the boilerplate code.

  3. The Reader Must Have the Plugin: If you compress a dataset using an external plugin (like Zstd or LZ4), any application that opens that file must also have the corresponding HDF5 plugin installed. If you are generating files for external users and cannot guarantee they have these plugins installed, use the built-in gzip filter for maximum portability.

Filter Implementation Details

When applying a filter via H5Pset_filter(plist_id, filter_id, flags, cd_nelmts, cd_values), you must pass an array of unsigned int values known as cd_values (Client Data Values). These values configure the specific behavior of the compressor.

Below are the explicit configurations and examples for every filter bundled with hdf5lib.

1. GZIP / Deflate

Recommendation: Use for Maximum Portability. GZIP is built directly into the core HDF5 library, meaning files compressed with it can be read by any standard HDF5 installation globally without needing external plugins. However, it is significantly slower than modern alternatives.

  • Filter ID: H5Z_FILTER_DEFLATE (1)
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 1
  • cd_values[0]: Compression level from 0 (none) to 9 (maximum).

You do not need to manually pack the cd_values array for GZIP. HDF5 provides a dedicated helper function.

// Apply GZIP compression with level 9
H5Pset_deflate(plist_id, 9);

2. Zstandard (Zstd)

Recommendation: Use as the Default General-Purpose Compressor. Developed by Facebook, Zstd provides compression ratios comparable to or better than GZIP, but at substantially faster compression and decompression speeds.

  • Filter ID: 32015
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 1
  • cd_values[0]: Compression level, from 1 (fastest) to 22 (best). Use 3 or 5 as a default; these provide an optimal balance of speed and file size, whereas levels above 10 offer steeply diminishing returns for significantly longer compression times.
unsigned int cd_values[1] = { 5 }; // Zstd level 5
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32015, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 1, cd_values);

3. LZ4

Recommendation: Use for Maximum Speed. LZ4 prioritizes extreme compression and decompression speeds (often bottlenecked only by RAM bandwidth) over finding the absolute smallest file size. Ideal for hot data, fast pipelines, or real-time I/O.

  • Filter ID: 32004
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 2
  • cd_values[0]: Reserved/padding (Pass 0).
  • cd_values[1]: Compression level. Passing 0 uses the standard, lightning-fast LZ4. Passing a value >0 (e.g., 9) enables LZ4-HC (High Compression) mode.
unsigned int cd_values[2] = { 0, 9 }; // LZ4 High Compression
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32004, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 2, cd_values);

4. Blosc2

Recommendation: Use for Parallel Compression and Complex Pipelines. Blosc2 splits each chunk into blocks and can (de)compress those blocks on several threads at once; see Multi-threading below. It also features a Programmable Filter Pipeline, allowing you to easily chain multiple pre-filters (like Delta followed by Bitshuffle) before the data hits the final compressor.

The plugin’s cd_values follow the layout of the reference HDF5-Blosc2 filter (the one hdf5plugin, PyTables and The HDF Group build) slot for slot, so other implementations can read, describe and append to hdf5lib’s datasets. The reference has room for a single pre-filter and no codec parameters, so the plugin packs the rest of its settings, the whole pre-filter pipeline and one parameter byte, into cd_values[0], which the reference only uses for its revision number and never reads.

Restrictions on ZFP: When using a ZFP compressor codec (33, 34, 35), the data must be float32 or float64 in native byte order (alone or in arrays). On any other datatype, a mandatory filter makes H5Dcreate2() fail and an optional one stores the data unfiltered. ZFP performs lossy compression directly on numerical values; if bytes are shuffled before ZFP, it corrupts the dataset. To ensure safety, this plugin automatically disables all Blosc2 pre-filters if a ZFP codec is selected. You must also ensure no upstream native HDF5 filters (e.g., H5Pset_shuffle) are applied before Blosc2 in your property list. ZFP also cannot store NaN or Inf values; see Non-finite values under ZFP. Chunks of more than 4 dimensions, or with a dimension under 4, are compressed as one long row, because the codec cannot take them as they are.

Plugin Configuration

  • Filter ID: 32026
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 7
Slot You pass The plugin stores
cd_values[0] The packed settings below The same, less anything that does not run (see below)
cd_values[1] 0 0: Blosc2 picks the block size
cd_values[2] 0 The item size in bytes
cd_values[3] 0 The chunk size in bytes
cd_values[4] Compression level, 0 to 9 The same, or 255 for a dataset a ZFP codec cannot take
cd_values[5] 0, or the code of the last pre-filter The code of the last pre-filter
cd_values[6] Codec The same
cd_values[7], [8...] Nothing The chunk rank and shape, for chunks compressed as B2ND arrays

The packed settings in cd_values[0]:

Bits Contents
31-24 0xB2, marking the value as hdf5lib’s
23-20 Layout version, 1
19-16 Pre-filter bitmask
15-8 Meta value
7-0 1, the reference filter’s revision

That is, cd_values[0] = 0xB2100001 + (bitmask << 16) + (meta << 8).

  • Pre-filter bitmask: the sum of the pre-filters to chain. They run in the order trunc-prec, delta, then bitshuffle or shuffle, whatever the order of the bits:
    • 1 = Byte Shuffle
    • 2 = Bitshuffle (wins if both 1 and 2 are given)
    • 4 = Delta
    • 8 = Truncate Precision (native-order float32 and float64 data, and arrays of them, only; the plugin drops it for every other datatype, which it would corrupt)
  • Meta value: one byte, read according to the configuration:
    • Truncate Precision: If the bitmask includes 8, the number of mantissa bits to keep: 1 to 23 for float32, 1 to 52 for float64. Blosc2 reads it as a signed byte, so a negative value (256 - n) drops n bits instead. A value that would keep no bits or drop the whole mantissa makes H5Dcreate2() fail; one that keeps more bits than the mantissa holds keeps them all.
    • NDLZ: The cell size, 4 or 8. Any other value is taken as 4.
    • ZFP Metadata: Blosc2 applies specific internal formulas to map this byte to ZFP’s floating-point parameters:
      • Precision (34): Passed directly as an integer. For 16 bits of precision, pass 16.
      • Accuracy (33): Interpreted as a base-10 exponent (10^meta). To pass a negative exponent like -3 (for an accuracy tolerance of 0.001), pass its 8-bit unsigned equivalent: 256 - 3 = 253.
      • Rate (35): Interpreted as a percentage of the original data size. For example, to achieve a rate of 8 bits per value on 32-bit floats, the compressed output must be exactly 25% of the original size (8 / 32 = 0.25), so you pass 25.
    • Otherwise, pass 0.
  • cd_values[4]: Compression level (0 to 9). A higher level makes H5Dcreate2() fail; the plugin itself records 255 for a dataset a ZFP codec cannot take, so that every chunk is stored unfiltered.
  • cd_values[5]: the last pre-filter that runs, as a single Blosc2 filter code, which is what the reference filter keeps in this slot: 2 if the bitmask has bitshuffle, else 1 if shuffle, else 3 if delta, else 4 if trunc-prec, else 0. The plugin works it out from the bitmask, so pass 0 or that code; any other value makes H5Dcreate2() fail with a message naming the code expected.
  • cd_values[6]: Compressor ID (0=blosclz, 1=lz4, 2=lz4hc, 4=zlib, 5=zstd, 32=ndlz, 33=zfp_acc, 34=zfp_prec, 35=zfp_rate).

The list the plugin stores records only what runs, so it may differ from the one you passed. The ZFP codecs and NDLZ skip the pre-filters, so their bitmask and cd_values[5] are stored as 0. With bitshuffle, the shuffle bit is dropped; truncate-precision is dropped on data it cannot take, or when it would keep every bit. The meta value is stored as 0 when nothing reads it, and NDLZ’s as 4 or 8. For chunks of 2 to 16 dimensions the plugin adds the rank and shape in cd_values[7] onwards, as the reference does, except for array datatypes, which it compresses as plain Blosc2, and ZFP chunks of more than 4 dimensions or with a dimension under 4, which it compresses as one long row. NDLZ always records the 2-D byte image it compresses. Values you pass after cd_values[6] are ignored.

Example 1: Standard Compression

Using Zstd (level 5) with the standard Bitshuffle pre-filter.

// cd_values[0]: bitmask 2 (Bitshuffle), meta 0 -> 0xB2120001
// cd_values[5]: Bitshuffle (2) is the last pre-filter
unsigned int cd_values[7] = { 0xB2120001, 0, 0, 0, 5, 2, 5 };
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32026, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 7, cd_values);

Example 2: Multi-Filter Pipeline

Chaining the Delta filter and Bitshuffle before hitting Zstd (level 5).

// cd_values[0]: bitmask Delta (4) + Bitshuffle (2) = 6, meta 0 -> 0xB2160001
// cd_values[5]: Bitshuffle (2) runs last
unsigned int cd_values[7] = { 0xB2160001, 0, 0, 0, 5, 2, 5 };
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32026, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 7, cd_values);

Example 3: Truncate Precision Pipeline

Truncating floats to 16 bits of precision, applying Bitshuffle, and compressing with LZ4.

// cd_values[0]: bitmask Truncprec (8) + Bitshuffle (2) = 10, meta 16 bits -> 0xB21A1001
// cd_values[5]: Bitshuffle (2) runs last
unsigned int cd_values[7] = { 0xB21A1001, 0, 0, 0, 5, 2, 1 };
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32026, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 7, cd_values);

Truncation zeroes the low bits of every value, including the payload bits of a NaN. Inf, and a NaN whose payload has its top bit set (the usual quiet NaN), come through unchanged, but R’s NA_real_ (bits 0x7FF00000000007A2) does not. Its payload sits in the low 11 bits, so keeping 41 or fewer bits of a float64 turns NA into Inf, and keeping 42 to 50 bits turns it into a plain NaN. To keep NA, leave truncation off for data that contains it.

Example 4: Blosc2 + ZFP Precision

Using Blosc2’s meta-compressor to run ZFP in Fixed Precision mode, keeping exactly 16 bits of precision.

// cd_values[0]: bitmask 0 (ZFP skips pre-filters), meta 16 bits -> 0xB2101001
unsigned int cd_values[7] = { 0xB2101001, 0, 0, 0, 5, 0, 34 };
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32026, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 7, cd_values);

Example 5: Blosc2 + ZFP Accuracy

Using ZFP Accuracy mode to enforce an absolute error tolerance of 0.001 (10^-3).

// ZFP Accuracy uses an exponent. The unsigned 8-bit equivalent of -3 is 253 (0xFD).
// cd_values[0]: bitmask 0, meta 253 -> 0xB210FD01
unsigned int cd_values[7] = { 0xB210FD01, 0, 0, 0, 5, 0, 33 };
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32026, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 7, cd_values);

Example 6: Blosc2 + ZFP Rate

Using ZFP Rate mode to compress 32-bit floats down to exactly 8 bits per value.

// ZFP Rate requires a percentage of the original size. 8 / 32 = 0.25 (25%).
// cd_values[0]: bitmask 0, meta 25 (0x19) -> 0xB2101901
unsigned int cd_values[7] = { 0xB2101901, 0, 0, 0, 5, 0, 35 };
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32026, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 7, cd_values);

Lists in other forms

The plugin reads cd_values[0] to tell what kind of list it was handed, both from your H5Pset_filter() call and from a creation property list copied from another dataset (as h5repack and H5Dget_create_plist() hand them on), and converts each to the layout above:

  • 0: the form earlier versions of hdf5lib documented, still accepted: { 0, 0, 0, 0, level, bitmask, codec, meta }, with the pre-filter bitmask in cd_values[5] and the meta value as an optional 8th value. Example 3 in this form is { 0, 0, 0, 0, 5, 10, 1, 16 }, and it stores exactly the same list as Example 3. Here cd_values[5] is still the bitmask, not a filter code. The option tuples hdf5plugin’s Blosc2() builds also start with 0, so they are read this way too, and two of its codes mean something else: 3 (its DELTA) is shuffle + bitshuffle, so bitshuffle, and 4 (its TRUNC_PREC) is delta. Passing no values at all also lands here: level 5, shuffle, BloscLZ.
  • 1: the reference filter’s own lists, such as a creation property list copied from a dataset h5py wrote. cd_values[5] is one filter code (0 none, 1 shuffle, 2 bitshuffle, 3 delta, 4 trunc-prec); there is no meta value, so trunc-prec fails H5Dcreate2() on native floats (it has no precision to keep) and NDLZ uses 4 x 4 cells. Any other code fails H5Dcreate2().
  • 2: lists stored by hdf5lib 2.1.1.0 to 2.2.0.0 (and development builds of 2.2.0.1): the bitmask in the low byte of cd_values[5], and the meta value in its next byte (lists of 7 values) or after the chunk shape.
  • 0xB2...: the layout above. A layout version other than 1 fails H5Dcreate2().

Any other cd_values[0] fails H5Dcreate2(). When the plugin compresses chunks for a dataset already in a file, such as one being appended to, it reads the stored list the same way: a dataset an earlier hdf5lib wrote keeps the settings it recorded, and one another implementation wrote gets the single pre-filter its cd_values[5] names, as the reference filter would run it. It refuses to compress with a layout version it does not know. Reading does not depend on any of these settings, because every Blosc2 chunk records its own pre-filters, codec and parameters.

What h5py sees

  • Reading: h5py with hdf5plugin reads every Blosc2 dataset hdf5lib writes, whatever the pre-filters and codec, as each chunk describes itself.
  • Describing: hdf5plugin.from_filter_options() describes datasets that use one of the five byte codecs as Blosc2(cname, clevel, filters), with filters the last pre-filter only, so Example 2 shows as BITSHUFFLE. It raises an error for NDLZ and the ZFP codecs.
  • Appending: h5py compresses the chunks it adds with the stored codec and level, but runs only the pre-filter in cd_values[5], without the meta value. Datasets whose last pre-filter is none, shuffle, bitshuffle or delta take new chunks without loss: Example 2’s new chunks are only bitshuffled, and Example 3’s are not truncated. Where trunc-prec runs alone, hdf5plugin has no precision to give it, so each chunk it compresses fails: a mandatory filter fails the write, and an optional one stores the chunk unfiltered, as hdf5plugin’s own Blosc2(filters=TRUNC_PREC) does. Writes to NDLZ datasets fail the same way. Writes to ZFP datasets either fail or, for chunks with recorded geometry, compress with a parameter of 0, which loses far more than the dataset was written with.

Multi-threading

The Blosc2 and Blosc (v1) filters use one thread by default. To use more, call hdf5lib_set_blosc_nthreads() (declared in hdf5lib.h) or set the BLOSC_NTHREADS environment variable. As everywhere in c-blosc, the environment variable takes precedence. Prefer the function: c-blosc2 also applies BLOSC_NTHREADS to the small bookkeeping contexts it creates for every chunk, and on Windows each of those then starts and stops threads of its own.

#include <hdf5lib.h>

hdf5lib_set_blosc_nthreads(4);           // use 4 threads from now on
int n = hdf5lib_get_blosc_nthreads();    // threads the filters will actually use
hdf5lib_set_blosc_nthreads(0);           // back to the default (BLOSC_NTHREADS, else 1)

Threads work on the blocks within a chunk, so they only help when a chunk holds several blocks. Blosc picks the block size from the codec and compression level. Zstd and zlib at Blosc level 9 (cd_values[4]), for example, use 1 MB blocks, so a 1 MB chunk is a single block and gains nothing from extra threads, while at level 5 the same chunk splits into four 256 KB blocks. Larger chunks or lower levels leave more room for parallelism. The worker threads are started on first use and kept between chunks, so they cost nothing per chunk once running.

Keep in mind that CRAN does not allow package examples, tests, or vignettes to use more than two threads. On Linux and macOS, a process forked from one that has already used Blosc2 threads (a parallel::mclapply() worker, say) runs the Blosc2 filter single-threaded.

5. ZFP

Recommendation: Use for High-Speed Lossy Compression. ZFP mathematically simplifies multidimensional arrays to achieve massive compression ratios. Use when perfect bit-for-bit reconstruction is not required.

Restrictions: ZFP strictly requires numeric, multidimensional arrays (natively supporting 32/64-bit integers and 32/64-bit floats). Any filter applied to the data before it reaches ZFP will completely corrupt the dataset. You must not apply upstream HDF5 pre-filters (e.g., Shuffle, Bitshuffle, Scale-Offset) before ZFP in your property list.

ZFP also needs the datatype in native byte order, and chunks with one to four dimensions longer than one. A single-value chunk, or a 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 one, does not qualify. On other datasets, a mandatory ZFP filter makes H5Dcreate2() fail. An optional one (see Non-finite values for how to make it optional) stays in the dataset’s filter pipeline but refuses every chunk, so HDF5 stores the data unfiltered and any reader can read it without ZFP.

(Note: While ZFP can be invoked as a codec within the Blosc2 meta-compressor, doing so restricts it to floating-point data only and limits the available compression modes to Accuracy, Precision, and Rate. For integer arrays, Expert mode, or Reversible (lossless) mode, you must use this standalone ZFP plugin).

The ZFP Modes Explained Simply

  • Fixed Accuracy: Defines a strict absolute error tolerance. Passing 3 ensures no decompressed value deviates from the original by more than 10−310^{-3} (0.001), regardless of whether the number is huge or tiny.

  • Fixed Precision: Defines a sliding scale of detail. Passing 16 keeps roughly 5 digits of detail scaled proportionally to the size of the number, allowing larger absolute errors on massive numbers and tiny absolute errors on microscopic fractions.

  • Fixed Rate: Defines a strict storage limit. Passing 8 forces the compressor to use exactly 8 bits of storage per value, guaranteeing a highly predictable file size.

  • Expert: Allows manual configuration of the underlying ZFP parameters (minbits, maxbits, maxprec, minexp) for advanced users requiring highly specific encoding profiles.

  • Reversible: Provides perfectly lossless compression, guaranteeing exact bit-for-bit reconstruction of the original numerical array.

Plugin Configuration

  • Filter ID: 32013
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 6
  • cd_values[0]: The compression mode (1=Rate, 2=Precision, 3=Accuracy, 4=Expert, 5=Reversible/Lossless).
  • cd_values[1-5]: Mode-specific parameters. For instance, in Precision mode (cd_values[0]=2), cd_values[2] specifies the bits of precision to keep, padding the rest with zeros (e.g., {2, 0, 16, 0, 0, 0}). Rate and Accuracy take a double, whose 8 bytes fill cd_values[2] and cd_values[3] in native memory order, as LLNL’s H5Z-ZFP and hdf5plugin lay it out.

While you can manually pack the 6-element cd_values array, the ZFP plugin exposes convenient external helper functions that you can declare in your C code to set the parameters effortlessly.

// Declare the external helpers provided by the bundled ZFP plugin
extern herr_t H5Pset_zfp_rate(hid_t plist, double rate);
extern herr_t H5Pset_zfp_precision(hid_t plist, unsigned int prec);
extern herr_t H5Pset_zfp_accuracy(hid_t plist, double acc);
extern herr_t H5Pset_zfp_expert(hid_t plist, unsigned int minbits, unsigned int maxbits, unsigned int maxprec, int minexp);
extern herr_t H5Pset_zfp_reversible(hid_t plist); // Lossless mode

// ... later in your code ...

// Compress data using ZFP's Accuracy mode (maintaining 0.001 tolerance)
H5Pset_zfp_accuracy(plist_id, 0.001);

Non-finite values

ZFP’s lossy modes have no encoding for NaN or Inf (or R’s NA, which is a NaN). Left alone, ZFP would turn each one into an arbitrary finite number and distort the other values in its block. So both the standalone ZFP filter and Blosc2’s ZFP codecs refuse any chunk that contains one, and what happens next depends on how the filter was added:

  • Optional (H5Z_FLAG_OPTIONAL): HDF5 stores just that chunk unfiltered. The data stays exact and the file reads normally; every other chunk is still compressed.
  • Mandatory (H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY): the write fails with an HDF5 error instead of storing corrupted values. HDF5 compresses chunks that fit in its chunk cache only when they are evicted or flushed, so the error may not appear until H5Dclose(). Check its return value, because HDF5 drops the chunk that failed.

The H5Pset_zfp_*() helpers add ZFP as a mandatory filter, as the upstream H5Z-ZFP plugin does. To get the per-chunk fallback, switch it to optional afterwards:

H5Pset_zfp_accuracy(plist_id, 0.001);
H5Pmodify_filter(plist_id, 32013, H5Z_FLAG_OPTIONAL, 0, NULL);

Reversible mode is lossless for every bit pattern, NaN and Inf included, so it accepts such chunks and compresses them as usual.

6. Bitshuffle

Recommendation: Use to Boost Compression of Structured Data. Bitshuffle is not a standalone compressor; it is a pre-filter that transposes the bits in structured arrays (like integers, floats, or compound datatypes) to expose redundancy, before handing that data off to an internal compressor (LZ4 or Zstd). It vastly improves compression ratios for highly structured datasets.

  • Filter ID: 32008
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 3
  • cd_values[0]: Block size. Pass 0 to let the library choose the optimal default (usually 1024).
  • cd_values[1]: Compressor algorithm. 0 = raw bitshuffling (no compression), 2 = LZ4, 3 = Zstd.
  • cd_values[2]: Compression level. Only applies if Zstd is selected (e.g., 5). Pass 0 for uncompressed or LZ4.
// Bitshuffle data, then apply Zstd compression at level 5
unsigned int cd_values[3] = { 0, 3, 5 }; 
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32008, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 3, cd_values);

7. Blosc (v1)

Recommendation: Use for Backwards Compatibility. Blosc v1 was a pioneering meta-compressor, but it has been entirely superseded by Blosc2 (which is faster, smarter, and supports more features). This filter is bundled strictly to ensure backward compatibility for reading older HDF5 files. Use Blosc2 for all new development.

  • Filter ID: 32001
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 7
  • cd_values[0-3]: Reserved (Pass 0).
  • cd_values[4]: Compression level (0 to 9). Note: Blosc enforces a universal 0-9 scale. If you select a codec with a wider range like Zstd, Blosc internally maps this 0-9 value to Zstd’s 1-22 scale.
  • cd_values[5]: Pre-filter (0=nofilter, 1=byte shuffle, 2=bit shuffle).
  • cd_values[6]: Compressor ID (0=blosclz, 1=lz4, 2=lz4hc, 3=snappy, 4=zlib, 5=zstd).
// Blosc v1 using LZ4 (level 5) and the standard byte shuffle pre-filter
unsigned int cd_values[7] = { 0, 0, 0, 0, 5, 1, 1 }; 
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32001, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 7, cd_values);

8. SZIP

Recommendation: Use for Backwards Compatibility. Historically used in legacy NASA and Earthdata datasets, the original SZIP algorithm carried strict licensing encumbrances that stifled widespread adoption. Modern tools like ZFP or Blosc2 are vastly superior for scientific data. This is included primarily for reading legacy archives (note: hdf5lib safely circumvents historical licensing issues by bundling libaec, a permissively licensed, drop-in replacement).

Restrictions: SZIP strictly requires numeric data (integers or floating-point numbers). It does not support compound datatypes, strings, or variable-length arrays. The chunk size (in elements) must also be an exact multiple of the block size.

  • Filter ID: H5Z_FILTER_SZIP (4)
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 2
  • cd_values[0]: Options mask (e.g., H5_SZIP_NN_OPTION_MASK or H5_SZIP_EC_OPTION_MASK).
  • cd_values[1]: Pixels per block. Must be even, typically 8, 16, or 32.

Like GZIP, SZIP has a dedicated helper function.

// Apply SZIP compression (Entropy Coding method, 8 pixels per block)
H5Pset_szip(plist_id, H5_SZIP_EC_OPTION_MASK, 8);

9. BZIP2

Recommendation: Use for Backwards Compatibility. While BZIP2 historically offered fantastic compression ratios, it is notoriously slow to compress and decompress. Zstd now achieves comparable or better ratios in a fraction of the time. Bundled strictly to allow reading of legacy archives.

  • Filter ID: 307
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 1
  • cd_values[0]: Block size / Compression level from 1 (fastest) to 9 (best). Default is 9.
unsigned int cd_values[1] = { 9 }; // BZIP2 level 9
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 307, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 1, cd_values);

10. LZF & Snappy

Recommendation: Use for Backwards Compatibility. Both LZF and Snappy were early pioneers of extreme-speed compression. However, LZ4 generally outperforms them in modern environments. LZF is included primarily because it was the default high-speed compressor in early versions of the Python h5py library.

Both LZF and Snappy are extremely fast, low-overhead algorithms. They require zero configuration parameters.

  • LZF Filter ID: 32000
  • Snappy Filter ID: 32003
  • Elements (cd_nelmts): 0
// Apply Snappy compression
H5Pset_filter(plist_id, 32003, H5Z_FLAG_MANDATORY, 0, NULL);

Snappy’s chunk layout: HDF5’s filter registry assigns 32003 to snappy-cuda, so hdf5lib writes chunks in snappy-cuda’s layout, and the two read each other’s files. A chunk holds the uncompressed length and a block size of 32 KiB, both as varints, then each block as a 4-byte little-endian length followed by that block’s raw Snappy data. Every block but the last is full, as snappy-cuda’s GPU decoder requires. hdf5lib writes it with the bundled csnappy library, so no CUDA or GPU is needed. hdf5lib reads chunks in this layout with any block size, and still reads the single raw Snappy stream per chunk that hdf5lib 2.2.0.0 and earlier wrote. Those older releases cannot read Snappy chunks written by hdf5lib 2.2.0.1 or later.

h5py with hdf5plugin has no 32003 filter. Blosc’s snappy codec (filter 32001 with cd_values[6] = 3) is unrelated: it wraps Snappy in Blosc’s own container, and it is the way to share Snappy-compressed data with Python.

Dynamically Loading Additional External Filters

While hdf5lib bundles an extensive suite of filters, it cannot include every possible algorithm. For instance, high-performance filters like SZ3 or VBZ are not bundled in order to maintain the package’s strict C-only, zero-dependency footprint.

However, HDF5 supports dynamically loading these algorithms at runtime through its plugin mechanism. hdf5lib is fully compiled with the necessary flags to enable this feature.

How It Works for the User

  1. Install the Filter: The user obtains and installs the desired filter plugin (.so, .dylib, or .dll files).
  2. Set the Plugin Path: The user must tell the HDF5 library where to find the installed plugins by setting the HDF5_PLUGIN_PATH environment variable.

Once configured, any R package linking to hdf5lib can seamlessly read datasets using that external filter.

# Tell HDF5 where to find external filter plugins
Sys.setenv(HDF5_PLUGIN_PATH = "/opt/hdf5/plugins/")

# Now, any function that uses hdf5lib can decompress an SZ3 file automatically
